item.content:encoded:
This piece has improved since the first draft I read, but it still… like it still felt like it fell flat for me.

+ show block
– hide block

First of all, we spend about a third of the article before we even see the food. This third is spent giving us some character development (which is fine) and a lot of imagery of logistics which I felt really bogged down the pacing of the story. There's a mystery that's promised to the reader in the beginning, but the following passages don't do much in the way of ratcheting tension around that mystery. Mostly because the imagery feels disjoint from the nature of "what is up with the food?". Sure, there's some unexplained oddities but the details about the room and the trek there do not make me anymore curious about the food itself.

I think the flashbacks are definitely better at getting across the main theme, but I really wish this had varied the types of interactions more. They all feel like they play out the same "I could have reached out to someone, but I didn't", which could've been mixed up by changing the stakes (maybe instead of a romantic bond maybe he could've offered to reach out to help). I understand that the third one is not necessarily romantic, but its so vague and ambiguous what he is failing to reach out for that it didn't really feel like a variation.

I actually liked the parental one in the beginning for variation, we don't get a lot of expansion on that, so again I didn't really latch onto it as well.

So, like coming into the ending I will be honest, I didn't feel particularly invested in this character. I think it has something to do with how direct the messaging is, which I know is something I brought up but I was hoping it would be addressed by reworking the flashbacks rather than just telling the reader directly. I prefer this to the theme being unclear, but it still doesn't suck me into the piece.

But really, what gets me about this article is the same thing that gets me about the other Waldon Studio format: the use of the overall review at the end feels like it actively undermines the emotionality of the piece.

The last thing the reader is left with isn't "this is my last food review" or "A life changing experience that I would not wish upon anyone". The last words are "Four stars". I believe the last version of this I read made the experience one star which made much more sense to me. Mostly because, this is what you're ending on, and apparently this "life changing experience" was not enough to elicit either extreme of the spectrum. The idea that there could be more in the tank, that there is something for this man above "losing his passion for food" that he can't bring himself to use either extreme of the scale actively undercuts the intense emotions we're supposed to be feeling at the end of the piece.

In fact, saying it was four stars would imply he enjoyed the whole affair, which again, does not track.

Even if it is because he's only rating the food and not the whole experience, such a half-measured line feels like a disservice to the piece, and heavily cheapens the emotions we feel prior.

-1

See, it I had ended this comment on a novote, it would've undercut how strongly I feel about the piece.

item.title: (no title)
item.content:encoded:
Oh I know the formatting is intended to be used for Ambrose articles and so I don’t fault the article for looking the same, it’s more they start and end in similar places and both revolve around a meal creating existential crisis in the reviewer, and other similar plot points.

For me, I would’ve distanced my article as much as possible for that reason… but maybe that’s just a me thing.

item.title: (no title)
item.content:encoded:
I'm sorry you felt that way! It's something I went back and forth on alot while writing, but ultimately determined the differences where great enough.

The endpoint of both stories is similar! That I can't deny - "broken person returns home". But the reasons for this and the journey that they have taken to get there couldn't be more different - Eden saw the center of the universe and had her soul stolen. Sam looked back at a life long lived and could not handle what they had seen.

I would be remiss if I didn't point at least one thing out though - the formatting is the Inkblot 9 theme (http://www.scpwiki.com/theme:inkblot), which was intended by Croquembouche to be a refresh of the Ambrose GoI format. So… Yes, the formatting and structural framing of "food critic review" are very similar, as self-similar as any two GoI formats are.

item.title: (no title)
item.content:encoded:
This is far too close to the contest entry upon which is cribs the formatting, so much so that I would assume it would not exist if not for the contest entry. Now, being inspired by something else is part of the creative process… but this is not inspiration. The plot, the style of writing, even the character feels too much like the entry from Crom.

The opening splash could be the same article, in that the wording is so similar. I realize many actual reviews are worded in a similar manner… but this isn’t an actual review, it’s a piece of fiction.

There’s even a bit about a sausage roll cart, which I’m fairly sure is also a plot point in the entry. I do not begrudge anyone from enjoying this but I felt like this was an attempt to recreate another article in slightly different fashion. And as such, it is not for me.

-1

item.content:encoded:
Thank you ever so! It's only due to the foresight of my kind critters that the latter half is as grounded as it is - it was originally even more abstract!

But given how abstract the themes are, it was something I was having issues with, keeping everything realistic and easy to track. It's not easy to make literal the slow and methodical destruction of someone's happiness!

I will say that the Croquembouche segment works on a literal and abstract level, and that figure stuck in the quagmire is identified in the piece!

I would say that the first half did a great job of building up the tension, and the second half was good, but maybe a tad too abstracted. I think it needs to be more grounded for it to be as engaging as the first half. Still, the energy and emotion expressed in this piece was phenomenal!

I am looking forward to the Ambrose Renaissance.

item.content:encoded: The first half of this is slow but engrossing, it's a nice pace and cadence to see in an article. Initially, I felt it was a bit too slow and meandering, but the second half more than makes up for it; it pays off on that build-up exceptionally well. To a certain extent, I still think it could be a bit more direct, but the strength of the writing makes that feel like an unnecessary nitpick in the grand scheme of things. This is good stuff. +1

item.title: Author Post
item.content:encoded:
So after reading Croquembouche's sublime Ambrose Vienna while being very unsober, I got inspired to write the version that I wanted to see - something a bit less clean cut, more concerned with the implications of something being taken from this reviewer. I also wanted the mental imagery of a pile of profiteroles performing a rendition of Bob Dylan's Hurricane, but that was lost in the editing.

It went through a lot of changes, and largely for the better, leaving us with what I like to think is a cross-section of someone looking back over their life, seeing the cumulative choices that they have made, and being destroyed by it.

A hearty thanks to Croquembouche, Captain Kirby, UraniumEmpire, and Gaffsey for their feedback on this. And a double thanks to Croquembouche for all his CSS help, without which this article would not be what it is.
